sections.overview: Allobates wayuu is a tiny ground-dwelling frog in the family Aromobatidae; it was originally described as Colostethus wayuu. It is known only from the Serranía de la Macuira in La Guajira, northern Colombia, and is endemic to that country.
sections.identification: The smooth body is brown, with cream limbs and lips, darker flanks, pale dorsolateral stripes and a cream belly flecked gray-brown; the hind limbs have dark bars. The original description reports snout-to-vent lengths of 13.6–16.1 mm in males and 15.8–19.7 mm in females; the ranges overlap. These are body lengths, not standing heights; no standard width or body mass is reported for either sex. Toe discs are expanded and toes partly webbed, while the fingers are unwebbed.
sections.habitat: Records place it between 210 and 780 m elevation around its type locality in Macuira National Natural Park. The mountain range contains a patchwork of dry tropical, thorn, gallery, deciduous and low-elevation cloud forests; the species is associated with dry and subhumid forest settings, but its precise microhabitat is not well mapped.
sections.diet: A Colombian biodiversity collection describes it as insectivorous, feeding on small invertebrates. No species-specific prey inventory was available in the sources consulted, so more detailed claims about preferred prey would be uncertain.
sections.behavior: The species is described as terrestrial and diurnal. Its brown, pale-striped pattern is generally cryptic against leaf litter, while a Colombian review reports that males darken overall during calling and that the pale dorsolateral stripes become more conspicuous; that color change is based on field observations rather than a dedicated experiment.
sections.reproduction: It lays eggs on land among leaf litter or near small pools. After hatching, the male carries roughly four to ten tadpoles on his back to water, where they continue development; these details come from Colombian natural-history records, and the species’ breeding calendar remains poorly documented.
sections.ecology: Its known range lies within a protected mountain landscape that links dry forest, gallery forest and cloud-forest patches. The park authority lists A. wayuu among the reserve’s endemic amphibians, but this designation should not be read as proof that every suitable habitat patch has been surveyed.
sections.conservation: The 2017 IUCN assessment changed its global category from Vulnerable to Least Concern; the assessment table records that category change. Despite that status, its documented range remains exceptionally restricted to the Macuira area, and the available sources do not establish a current population trend or a measured threat level.
